primary_text_note: In copyright (Winterson, 1985). Verified against the full text of the novel (PDF at marul.ffst.hr/~bwillems/fymob/oranges.pdf, grepped, never read whole) plus LitCharts chapter summaries, SparkNotes Judges, Wikipedia and Goodreads/bookquoters quote collections. GradeSaver and Course Hero were unreachable (403).

findings.field: content_html / exam_tip_html / knowledge_checks / flashcard_questions / glossary_terms / practice_questions
findings.claim: "For Eduqas C720U Component 2, Section A, the exam gives you an extract and two questions worth 40 marks total. Part (a) (20 marks) tests AO1 and AO2 ... Part (b) (20 marks) tests AO1, AO2, and AO4 ... For post-1914 texts, AO3 (comparison) is not assessed." Repeated in the L1 exam tip, revision tip, glossary AO4 entry, a knowledge check, two flashcards, and again across L8 (exam technique, exam tip, three flashcards, glossary).
findings.truth: The post-1914 prose section is ONE source-based question worth 40 marks, with an extract printed on the paper. There is no part (a)/(b) and no 20+20 split. The section assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4 only. AO4 is not context: the spec defines AO4 as 'use a range of vocabulary and sentence structures for clarity, purpose and effect, with accurate spelling and punctuation'. AO3 is the context objective and it is NOT assessed in this section, so telling students that context earns marks here is mark-affecting.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md lines 405-425 (Section A (20%) Post 1914 Prose/Drama, 40 marks, source based response, 'Section A assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4', closed book) and lines 480-495 (AO definitions)

findings.claim: All 48 practice questions are labelled '20 marks - Extract Analysis' or '20 marks - Wider Text Response' with a 17-20 / 13-16 / 9-12 / 5-8 / 1-4 ladder (L5-L8 collapse it to 'Band 4-1').
findings.truth: The question is worth 40 marks. Relabelled to '40 marks - Source-based response' and rescaled to the 33-40 / 25-32 / 17-24 / 9-16 / 1-8 ladder used by the sibling Eduqas post-1914 units. 'Band 4-1' is not a band on this qualification.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md line 407 '(40 marks)'; sibling unit scripts/_retrofc/units/english-literature-eduqas__the-woman-in-black/_edits.json

findings.claim: Board named in student-facing text: heading 'The Eduqas Exam: What You Need to Know' (L1), 'Eduqas C720U' (L1), 'Eduqas Component 2 Section A' (L8 description and L8 flashcard), 'Which AOs are assessed in Eduqas Part (a)' (L1 flashcard), 'What AOs does Eduqas assess in Part (a)' (L8 flashcard).
findings.truth: House rule: Eduqas lessons never name the board. The project validator also rejects the spec-code and 'Component N' patterns outright (scripts/_validate_content_json.py BANNED_PATTERNS), so the unit currently fails that gate.
findings.evidence: CLAUDE.md house rule; scripts/_validate_content_json.py BANNED_PATTERNS

findings.claim: "She had given me to the Lord... like Samuel." plus 'The biblical allusion to Samuel - a child dedicated to God's service from birth'. Also two flashcards.
findings.truth: Fabricated. The word 'Samuel' does not appear anywhere in the novel. The real passage is the mother's dream: 'She would get a child, train it, build it, dedicate it to the Lord: a missionary child, a servant of God, a blessing.'
findings.evidence: Full text, Genesis: 'My mother, out walking that night, dreamed a dream ... She would get a child, train it, build it, dedicate it to the Lord'. Grep for 'Samuel' returns nothing.

findings.claim: The mother's Enemies are quoted as "the next door neighbours, sex, slugs, and the French" (L2 content, L2 exam tip, L2 flashcard, L2 glossary, L7 content, L7 flashcard, L2 practice mark scheme), and the Friends list is paraphrased as 'the church congregation, the Bible, missionary work'.
findings.truth: Misquotation. The novel reads 'Enemies were: The Devil (in his many forms), Next Door, Sex (in its many forms), Slugs. Friends were: God, Our dog, Auntie Madge, The Novels of Charlotte Bronte, Slug pellets' - 'and me, at first.' The French are not in the list.
findings.evidence: Full text, Genesis, the Friends/Enemies lists.

findings.claim: "When Jeanette goes deaf (a real medical condition), her mother ignores it for months because she believes God will provide." Repeated in an L2 flashcard, in L7 content and in an L2 practice mark scheme.
findings.truth: Wrong. Nobody realises she is deaf. Jeanette assumes she is in a state of rapture and her mother assumes the same, telling the church it is 'the Lord' working in mysterious ways, so word goes round that the child must not be spoken to. Miss Jewsbury works it out and shouts in the hospital ward, 'This child's not full of the Spirit, she's deaf.'
findings.evidence: Full text, Exodus; LitCharts plot summary ('no one noticed, believing Jeanette to be in the throes of a divine episode').

findings.field: description / content_html / conclusion_html / knowledge_checks / flashcard_questions / glossary_terms / practice_questions
findings.claim: The unit repeatedly says the chapter in which Jeanette falls in love with Melanie is titled 'Leviticus', and builds an irony reading on Leviticus being the book of sexual law (L3 description, content, key fact, revision tip, conclusion, knowledge check, flashcard, practice question; L6 content twice, knowledge check, flashcard, practice mark scheme).
findings.truth: Melanie is met at the fish stall and the relationship develops in 'Numbers', the book of the Israelites wandering in the wilderness. 'Leviticus' is the Society for the Lost chapter: the market pitch, Mrs Arkwright, the perfection sermon and the prince's fairy tale. Melanie does not appear in Leviticus at all.
findings.evidence: LitCharts 3. Leviticus and 4. Numbers chapter summaries; full text.

findings.claim: "I loved her so much my stomach felt as though it were full of air." used as the key love quotation (L3 content, L3 flashcard, L3 practice mark scheme, L7 content, L7 practice mark scheme).
findings.truth: Fabricated. 'full of air' occurs once in the novel, in a simile for Melanie AFTER she repents: 'She looked tired and crumpled like a balloon full of old air.' Replaced with verbatim lines: Jeanette to Melanie, 'I love you almost as much as I love the Lord', and the physical 'the triangle of muscle in her stomach'.
findings.evidence: Full text; grep for 'full of air' and 'stomach'.

findings.claim: Jeanette is accused of harbouring "a demon" and of being under "the influence of the Devil." (L3 content and flashcard).
findings.truth: Misquotation. The pastor says the two girls 'have fallen under Satan's spell', 'have fallen foul of their lusts' and 'These children are full of demons.'
findings.evidence: Full text, Joshua.

findings.field: content_html / conclusion_html / exam_tip_html / knowledge_checks / flashcard_questions / practice_questions
findings.claim: "I couldn't understand what was happening. The hymns were too loud. The hands were too heavy." presented as the exorcism quotation, with a whole AO2 reading built on the repetition of 'too'. Used in L3 content, key fact, revision tip, exam tip, a fill-in knowledge check, two flashcards and a practice mark scheme. Also 'She is kept without food for days.'
findings.truth: Fabricated. Those sentences are not in the novel. The verifiable detail is the pastor's hand 'hot and heavy on my neck' while he tells the church she is 'full of demons', and then thirty-six hours locked in the parlour with a blanket, no food and no light bulb. The keyed answer 'heavy' survives on the real line.
findings.evidence: Full text, Joshua: 'His hand was hot and heavy on my neck'; 'Over the thirty-six hours that followed'; 'she took away the light bulb'.

findings.claim: The orange demon is quoted as saying "Everyone has a demon... The demon you get depends on the life you lead" (L3 content and flashcard), and is called a "small orange demon".
findings.truth: The second half is fabricated. Jeanette thinks 'Everyone has a demon like cats have fleas'; the demon then says 'the demon you get depends on the colour of your aura, yours is orange which is why you've got me.' The moral point changes: it is not earned by how you live.
findings.evidence: Full text, Joshua.

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'Where does Jeanette first meet Melanie?' answer 'At church - Melanie is a new convert Jeanette brings into the congregation.'
findings.truth: Wrong, and it contradicts the lesson's own content_html. Jeanette first sees Melanie at a market fish stall, boning a kipper; she only invites her to church later.
findings.evidence: Full text, Numbers; Wikipedia plot summary; L3 content_html paragraph n2.

findings.claim: "After the second exorcism attempt, the orange demon returns and tells Jeanette: 'To eat of the fruit means to leave the garden.'" Also L7 content, two knowledge checks, two flashcards and two practice questions attribute the line to the demon.
findings.truth: Misattributed and misplaced. There is no second exorcism and the demon does not return. The line is the narrator's, in the walled-garden allegory in the same chapter as the exorcism: 'To eat of the fruit means to leave the garden because the fruit speaks of other things, other longings.'
findings.evidence: Full text, Joshua, the Euphrates walled-garden passage.

findings.claim: "When the church discovers Jeanette's relationship with Katy, there is no second exorcism. Instead, Jeanette is expelled completely ... there is no offer of redemption ... She is not just sinful but 'unteachable'." Also a knowledge-check option and a flashcard.
findings.truth: 'Unteachable' is not in the novel and the account is wrong. Jeanette shields Katy by claiming the affair is still with Melanie. The church's ruling is that the fault is women holding power, so women are barred from preaching and teaching. They DO offer her the Bible class back, under supervision. She refuses to repent, the pastor declares her one of the people in Hebrews 'to whom it is impossible to speak the truth', and it is her mother who puts her out: 'You'll have to leave. I'm not havin' demons here.'
findings.evidence: Full text, Judges; SparkNotes Judges summary.

findings.claim: "I left and walked across the town to work driving an ice cream van (and later helping at a funeral parlour)." A flashcard quotes a different fabricated version of the same line ('to the ice cream factory').
findings.truth: Fabricated. The novel reads: 'I had gone back to work at the undertakers, or funeral parlour as the woman and her friend Joe preferred to call it ... Sometimes I had to park the ice-cream van round the back, lay some person out round the front, then get on with my round again.'
findings.evidence: Full text, Ruth.

findings.claim: "The mother is still controlling, still obsessive, but she makes Jeanette a cup of tea. This small gesture contains the novel's most complex emotional truth." Repeated in L8 content, an L8 knowledge-check option, two flashcards and two practice mark schemes.
findings.truth: Fabricated. The mother makes no cup of tea at the end; Jeanette is the one who asks for one. The closing beats are the mother's line over a glut of pineapple - "'After all,' said my mother philosophically, 'oranges are not the only fruit'" - and then her CB broadcast, 'This is Kindly Light calling Manchester.' The novel's title line is the one students should carry, not an invented gesture.
findings.evidence: Full text, Ruth, final pages.

findings.claim: The mother "adopted Jeanette as a 'weapon in the war against the world'" (L5) and "the mother names her 'a weapon in the war against the world'" (L8).
findings.truth: Fabricated. The phrase is not in the novel. The real wording is 'I had been brought in to join her in a tag match against the Rest of the World', and the plan is to 'get a child, train it, build it, dedicate it to the Lord'.
findings.evidence: Full text, Genesis.

findings.claim: "Pastor Finch represents institutional religious authority ... He leads the exorcism and pronounces the expulsion."
findings.truth: Wrong. Pastor Finch is a visiting preacher from Stockport with a demon-painted van; his contribution is the sermon that even 'this innocent child' could be 'a house of demons', which supplies the congregation's vocabulary. The unnamed local pastor denounces Jeanette from the pulpit and orders the lock-in; her mother puts her out of the house.
findings.evidence: Full text, Genesis / Numbers / Joshua / Judges; LitCharts Joshua summary ('The unnamed pastor (not Spratt or Finch) leads it').

findings.claim: "[Miss Jewsbury] approaches Jeanette after the exorcism offering shelter and ultimately a sexual relationship."
findings.truth: Wrong order. Miss Jewsbury takes Jeanette home on the night of the public denunciation, before the lock-in; they sleep together that night, and the elders confront Jeanette about it the next morning. The exorcism follows.
findings.evidence: Full text, Joshua; LitCharts Joshua summary.

findings.claim: "Joshua, about conquering the Promised Land, names the chapter where Jeanette is expelled."
findings.truth: Jeanette is put out of the house in 'Judges', not 'Joshua'. Joshua is the chapter of the public denunciation, the lock-in and the orange demon.
findings.evidence: LitCharts 6. Joshua and SparkNotes 7. Judges summaries; full text.

findings.claim: "The most significant [fairy tale] is the story of a princess who seeks a perfect jewel but discovers that perfection is an illusion. Another tells of a woman who must choose between a walled garden and the open world." Also the L6 exam tip and a practice question and its mark scheme.
findings.truth: Invented. The Leviticus tale is a PRINCE who searches for a flawless wife, writes 'The Holy Mystery of Perfection', finds a woman who tells him perfection is balance rather than flawlessness, and has her beheaded for saying so. The other long interpolation is Winnet Stonejar, bound to a sorcerer by an invisible thread, who has to leave his village.
findings.evidence: Full text, Leviticus and Deuteronomy/Ruth; LitCharts 3. Leviticus summary.

findings.claim: "Everyone who tells a story tells it differently... the important thing is to tell and retell." (L6 content and L8 content).
findings.truth: The second half is fabricated. The sentence reads: 'Everyone who tells a story tells it differently, just to remind us that everybody sees it differently.' The short form already quoted in the L6 key fact, conclusion and knowledge check is correct and is left alone.
findings.evidence: Full text, Deuteronomy; bookquoters.com quote collection.

findings.claim: "She always had an orange ready for me." (L7 content and flashcard).
findings.truth: Fabricated. The novel's line is the mother's flat answer to distress: "'You've got to,' she said. 'Here, have an orange.'" (and 'let's have an orange'). The symbol reading is unaffected; the quotation is not real.
findings.evidence: Full text, Exodus; grep for 'orange ready' returns nothing.

findings.claim: "It's not what happened, it's a story about what happened" is presented as a direct Winterson quotation in L1 content (twice), the L1 key fact, an L1 flashcard, an L1 practice mark scheme and L7 content.
findings.truth: The underlying claim - that Winterson insists the novel is fiction rather than autobiography - is well supported (she calls it 'semi-autobiographical' and writes in the 2014 Vintage introduction that she wanted to use herself 'as a fictional character - an expanded I'). The exact sentence could not be sourced to Winterson in any fetchable source. Not edited, per the unverified-quotation rule, but worth replacing with a sourced statement if the unit is revisited.
findings.evidence: Searches of jeanettewinterson.com, Wikipedia, SparkNotes context page and Goodreads quote pages did not return the sentence.

findings.claim: 'I miss God. I miss the company of someone utterly loyal.' is placed immediately after the exorcism in L3 ('She tells us: ...').
findings.truth: The quotation is verbatim and correctly attributed to Jeanette, but in the novel it comes much later, when she is grown and away from home, not in the aftermath of the exorcism. Not edited: the sentence around it does not actually assert a chapter.
findings.evidence: Full text: the passage runs 'where was God now, with heaven full of astronoughts, and the Lord overthrown? I miss God...'

summary: Every lesson carries at least one mark-affecting error. The exam frame is wrong throughout (an invented two-part 20+20 question, AO4 defined as context, the board named, all 48 practice questions labelled 20 marks), and thirteen quotations are fabricated or misquoted, including the Enemies list, the exorcism lines, the orange demon's rule, the leaving-home line and the novel's ending. Two chapter attributions are wrong (Melanie is in Numbers, not Leviticus; Jeanette is put out in Judges, not Joshua), and the Leviticus fairy tale is invented.
